questions.topic: Energy per quadratic degree of freedom
questions.learningObjective: State the average energy held by one quadratic degree of freedom
questions.stem: Ticket THRM-118 asks the platform team to state what average energy each quadratic degree of freedom of a gas holds at thermal equilibrium.

options.text: One full kT, since each quadratic term receives an equal share of the total energy.
options.misconception: thinks equipartition hands a full kT to each quadratic term

options.text: One half of kT, because the quadratic term appears together with its constant in the energy.
One quarter of kT, since the term can be positive or negative with equal likelihood.
options.misconception: halves the equipartition share again out of symmetry alone

options.text: No energy at all, since a quadratic term stores only shape and not thermal motion.
options.misconception: believes the potential term carries no thermal energy

questions.explanation: Equipartition gives every quadratic term an average contribution of one half of kT. Treating it as a full kT double counts, and the potential part of the term does hold thermal energy.
questions.hint: Each oscillator splits its energy between motion and position.

questions.topic: Mean kinetic energy of one gas molecule

questions.stem: Issue LAB-77 shows the team plotting mean kinetic energy per molecule against temperature for argon and for nitrogen, and both datasets fell on one straight line.

options.text: The two gases share the line because only translational motion contributes, and it depends on temperature alone.
The two gases share the line because their molecular masses are close enough for the curves to coincide.
options.misconception: attributes the shared slope to similar molar masses

options.text: The curves coincide because nitrogen molecules are smaller and therefore strike the walls more often.
options.misconception: blames smaller size for identical energies

options.text: The nitrogen curve must lie above argon because a diatomic molecule carries extra rotational energy.
options.misconception: counts rotational energy inside the translational mean

questions.explanation: The mean translational kinetic energy is (3/2)kT for every ideal gas, so the mass cancels out. Nitrogen's rotational energy lies outside the translational average and cannot lift the line.
questions.hint: The translational mean depends on temperature alone.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heat to warm a diatomic gas at constant volume
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the constant volume heat of a diatomic gas is n(5/2)R delta T
questions.stem: Query THRD-31 asks the team to explain, in writing, why heating a diatomic ideal gas at constant volume requires n(5/2)R delta T of heat.

answer.exemplar: A diatomic molecule has three translational and two rotational quadratic degrees of freedom, so equipartition gives it a total internal energy of (5/2)kT per molecule. The heat at constant volume equals the change in internal energy, and since the energy per kelvin per mole is (5/2)R, the heat needed is n(5/2)R delta T, provided the vibrational modes remain frozen out.

questions.explanation: At constant volume no work is done, so heat equals the change in internal energy. Three translational plus two rotational quadratic degrees of freedom give (5/2)nRT, which depends linearly on T.
questions.hint: Count the quadratic degrees of freedom first.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Mean kinetic energy of one gas molecule
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the mean molecular kinetic energy depends only on temperature
questions.stem: Question THR-52 asks the group to explain in writing why the mean kinetic energy of one gas molecule depends on temperature but not on the mass of the molecule.

answer.exemplar: For an ideal gas the mean translational kinetic energy per molecule is (3/2)kT, which follows from equipartition applied to the three translational quadratic terms (1/2)m vx squared, (1/2)m vy squared and (1/2)m vz squared. The mass multiplies the velocity squared, so heavy molecules move more slowly and their larger momentum transfer balances the smaller speed. Temperature alone therefore fixes the mean energy of every molecule, and a heavier gas at the same temperature has the same mean energy but a lower speed and a higher density.

questions.explanation: Equipartition gives each translational quadratic term half of kT, so mass cancels from the mean energy. Heavier molecules thus move more slowly at the same temperature, and heavier gases are denser.
questions.hint: The translational mean depends on temperature alone.

options.text: The molar heat capacity is 25.0 J per mol K, close to 3R, so the Dulong-Petit law fits.
The molar heat capacity is 2.56 J per mol K, so the Dulong-Petit law does not fit the data.
options.misconception: divides the heat by the temperature but not by the moles

options.text: The molar heat capacity is 25.0 J per mol K, and the law fits only because the sample is a liquid.
options.misconception: claims the phase of the sample explains the agreement

questions.explanation: Q over n delta T gives 48.0 divided by 0.150 times 12.8, that is 25.0 J per mol K, within a percent of 3R = 24.94. A value near R would mean one vibration per atom instead of the three the law assumes.
questions.hint: Divide the heat by moles and by the temperature rise.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Mean energy of a classical oscillator
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the mean energy of a classical oscillator is kT
questions.stem: Question OSC-40 asks the team to write out why the mean energy of a classical oscillator is exactly kT and to show where each half comes from.

answer.exemplar: A classical harmonic oscillator has a quadratic kinetic term (1/2)mv squared and a quadratic potential term (1/2)kx squared. Equipartition assigns one half of kT to each quadratic term, so the kinetic part contributes (1/2)kT and the potential part contributes (1/2)kT. Adding the two gives a total mean energy of kT per oscillator, independent of the mass m and the stiffness k, which is a striking and purely classical result.

questions.explanation: Equipartition splits the mean energy between the kinetic and potential quadratic terms, each getting half of kT, so the total is kT. Mass and stiffness change only how the split falls, never the total.
questions.hint: Split the mean energy between motion and position.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heat to warm a diatomic gas at constant volume
questions.learningObjective: Explain the constant volume heat capacity of a diatomic gas
questions.stem: Question GAS-33 asks the team to explain in writing why the constant volume molar heat capacity of a diatomic gas is (5/2)R, and to say what changes if the vibrational modes freeze out.

answer.exemplar: A diatomic molecule contributes three translational and two rotational quadratic degrees of freedom. Equipartition assigns half of kT to each, so the internal energy per molecule is (3/2 + 2/2)kT = (5/2)kT and the molar heat capacity at constant volume is (5/2)R. If the vibrational mode is frozen out at low temperature it is no longer quadratic in energy, the equipartition result no longer applies to it, and the molar heat capacity no longer climbs towards (5/2)R from above.

questions.explanation: The constant volume heat capacity is dU over dT, and equipartition gives (5/2)nRT for a diatomic gas. A frozen vibrational mode stops adding its R, so the heat capacity holds at (5/2)R instead of rising.
questions.hint: Heat capacity is the slope of the energy against temperature.

answer.exemplar: Dulong-Petit states that the molar heat capacity at constant volume of a crystalline solid approaches three times the gas constant, C = 3R = 24.94 J per mol K, one R for each of the three independent spatial vibrations of an atom. The law rests on classical equipartition, which assumes that every vibrational mode is active. At low temperature many modes are frozen out because the spacing between their energy levels exceeds kT, so they contribute less than R each and the measured heat capacity falls well below 3R.

questions.explanation: Three vibrations per atom, each contributing R classically, give the Dulong-Petit value 3R. At low temperature some modes freeze out because their level spacing exceeds kT, so the heat capacity falls below 3R.
questions.hint: Each atom has three spatial vibrations.

questions.topic: Energy per quadratic degree of freedom
questions.learningObjective: State the equipartition result for a classical gas in writing
questions.stem: Question EQP-5 asks the team to state the equipartition result for a classical gas in writing and to explain what each quadratic degree of freedom contributes.

answer.exemplar: Equipartition states that in a classical system at temperature T, each independent quadratic term in the energy contributes on average one half of kT per molecule, or R per mole. A monatomic ideal gas has three such translational terms, so its internal energy is (3/2)nRT and its molar heat capacity at constant volume is (3/2)R. The result depends only on the temperature and on the number of quadratic degrees of freedom, not on the masses, the stiffnesses or the interactions between particles.

questions.explanation: Equipartition gives half of kT to every quadratic term, so counting terms rather than atoms yields the energy. Each extra active quadratic degree of freedom adds R to the constant volume molar heat capacity.
questions.hint: Count quadratic terms rather than particles.

answer.exemplar: The classical harmonic oscillator has energy E = (1/2)mp squared plus (1/2)kx squared, and both terms are quadratic. questions.stem: Question EQP-18 asks the team to write out why equipartition results such as half of kT per quadratic degree of freedom apply only in the classical regime.

answer.exemplar: Equipartition follows from classical statistical mechanics, in which the energy of a quadratic term is averaged over a continuous distribution of values. That averaging is valid only when the level spacing of the mode is much smaller than kT, so the mode is thermally active. As the temperature falls, the spacing between the quantum levels of a mode grows relative to kT, the mode freezes out, and it contributes less than its classical share of kT. The classical formula then overestimates the energy, as happens with the vibrational modes of a solid at low temperature.

questions.explanation: Equipartition averages a quadratic term over continuous energies, which is justified only when the level spacing is small compared with kT. Below the freezing temperature a mode contributes less than its classical share.
questions.hint: Level spacing compared with kT decides.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Mean kinetic energy of one gas molecule
questions.learningObjective: Relate the mean molecular energy to the speed of heavier molecules
questions.stem: Task KIN-57 asks first for the mean kinetic energy of one neon atom at 300 K and then what a molecule of a much heavier gas must do at the same temperature to match it.

options.text: The mean is 6.21e-21 J, and the heavier molecule must move faster to keep the same mean energy.
options.misconception: thinks heavier molecules need more speed to match the energy

options.text: The mean is 6.21e-21 J, and the heavier molecule must move more slowly to keep the same mean energy.
The mean is 6.21e-21 J, and the heavier molecule must collide more often to keep the same mean energy.
options.misconception: confuses collision frequency with the mean kinetic energy

options.text: The mean is 6.21e-21 J, and the heavier molecule must carry the same speed to keep the same mean energy.
options.misconception: assumes equal energies imply equal speeds

questions.explanation: The mean is (3/2)kT = 1.5 times 1.380649e-23 times 300, that is 6.21e-21 J for every ideal gas. Since energy scales as mass times speed squared, heavier molecules must move more slowly to match it.
questions.hint: Energy scales as mass times speed squared.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Molar heat capacity of a solid
questions.learningObjective: Compare the molar heat capacities of a solid and a monatomic gas
questions.stem: Task MAT-30 asks which pair correctly compares the molar heat capacity of a solid metal with that of a monatomic gas.

options.text: The solid is (3/2)R and the monatomic gas is 3R, because solids always store more energy.
options.misconception: reverses the two heat capacities

options.text: The solid is 3R and the monatomic gas is (3/2)R, since the solid adds potential energy as well.
Both are 3R, because three quadratic terms are active in each case.
options.misconception: counts the solid's potential terms twice

options.text: The solid is (5/2)R and the monatomic gas is (3/2)R, because the solid is a diatomic solid.
options.misconception: borrows the diatomic gas count for a solid metal

questions.explanation: A solid atom has three vibrations, each with a kinetic and a potential quadratic term, giving 3R per mole, while a monatomic gas has only the three translational terms, giving (3/2)R.
questions.hint: The solid adds potential quadratic terms.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heat capacity of a metal mass
questions.learningObjective: Extract a specific heat capacity from laboratory heat data
questions.stem: Incident INC-8 lists a laboratory run in which 2.00 kg of metal absorbs 9.00e4 J for a 50.0 K rise, and the ticket asks for the specific heat capacity of that metal.

options.text: The specific heat capacity is 450 J per kg K, since the heat is shared equally between two identical samples.
options.misconception: divides the heat by an imagined second sample

options.text: The specific heat capacity is 1800 J per kg K, since the temperature rise must be halved for a Celsius scale.
options.misconception: confuses the Celsius scale with a halving of the energy

options.text: The specific heat capacity is 900 J per kg K, since Q over mass and over the rise gives 9.00e4 over 2.00 times 50.0.
The specific heat capacity is 90.0 J per kg K, since the mass in kilograms must be squared.
options.misconception: squares the mass when inverting the formula

questions.explanation: The specific heat capacity is Q over m delta T = 9.00e4 over 2.00 times 50.0, that is 900 J per kg K. The mass enters linearly and the temperature rise must be the 50.0 K change, not the final temperature.
questions.hint: Specific heat is heat per kilogram per kelvin.
